Sets and Set Operations

Discrete Mathematics · Chapter 2 · student-approved English edition

The prerequisites are the meaning of a proposition, quantifiers, and the basic equivalence laws from Chapter 1. This chapter covers extensional sets, membership and containment, finite and indexed set operations, power sets, products, finite cardinality, and the proof methods that connect them. Relations, functions, systematic counting, and induction are separate chapters. The worked bank is deliberately extensive: a difficult set question usually fails at an exact definition or boundary case, not at a missing formula.

1. Course selection and coverage contract

Four principal written courses were read and combined for this chapter: MIT 6.042J (Lehman, Leighton, Meyer, 2015, section 4.1; course instructors Meyer and Chlipala); Stanford CS103 (Amy Liu's Winter 2024 course archive, Guide to Proofs on Sets); Cornell CS2800 (Pass and Tseng, 2015, section 1.1); and Carnegie Mellon 15-151 (Sutner, 2022, the Set Operations and Cartesian Products slides). UC Berkeley CS70 Summer 2024 Note 0 was read as a fifth, supplemental text. MIT gives concise definitions and an elementwise distributive proof; Stanford explains proof construction; Cornell ties diagrams and products to computer-science notation; CMU supplies indexed families and subtle edge cases; Berkeley independently confirms the foundational notation. Exact links and review limits appear in References.

This is a bounded comparison of publicly accessible written course materials, not a claim to have searched every university course worldwide. No syllabus-only entry is counted as a read course. The topic and reasoning-pattern audit is recorded with the manuscript; it controls the scope and the solved-problem bank. Original Iranian MSc and PhD questions are now included under the student instruction of 3 October 2026. A finished chapter cannot mathematically guarantee a correct response to every unseen examination question, but the definitions, proofs, counterexamples, and solved problems below are designed to expose the identifiable failure modes in this chapter boundary.

2. Objects, membership, and equality

2.1 What a set asserts

A set is an unordered collection with no repeated members. The notation x ∈ A means that object x is a member of set A; x ∉ A means it is not. Thus {2,1,2} = {1,2}, whereas (1,2) and (2,1) are different ordered pairs. A set may contain other sets: ∅, {∅}, and {{∅}} are three different objects. The empty set ∅ has no members; the singleton {∅} has one member, namely ∅. Therefore ∅ ∈ {∅}, ∅ ⊆ {∅}, and ∅≠{∅}. The first statement is membership, the second containment, and neither can replace the other.

For any sets A and B, extensional equality means exactly the same members:

A = B ⇔ ∀x (x ∈ A ↔ x ∈ B).

This is the most reliable route to an identity. Prove both A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A, or prove the membership biconditional directly. A Venn diagram can suggest an identity or show a counterexample region, but a correctly quantified elementwise argument proves it. Reordering or repeating entries in roster notation never changes a set.

Set-builder notation {x ∈ D : P(x)} selects those elements of a specified domain D for which P is true. For example, {n ∈ ℤ : n2<10} = {−3,−2,−1,0,1,2,3}. The displayed domain matters: {x ∈ ℝ : x2 = 2} and {x ∈ ℚ : x2 = 2} are not equal. Unrestricted phrases of the form “the set of every object satisfying P” can lead to Russell's paradox; in this course, set-builder notation always uses a specified ambient set or an accepted construction. This caution is about legitimate set formation, not a computational procedure.

2.2 Subsets, proper subsets, and their logical form

A ⊆ B means every member of A belongs to B: ∀x(x ∈ A → x ∈ B). The relation is reflexive (A ⊆ A) and transitive (A ⊆ B and B ⊆ C imply A ⊆ C). It is antisymmetric: A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A imply A = B. A ⊊ B means A ⊆ B and A≠B, equivalently A ⊆ B and some b ∈ B ∖ A exists. The symbol ⊂ is used inconsistently across books, so this chapter always writes ⊆ or ⊊ .

The empty set is a subset of every set, including itself, because there is no counterexample x ∈ ∅ with x ∉ A. It is a proper subset of A precisely when A is nonempty. Membership does not transfer to containment: 2 ∈ {1,2}, but 2 ⊆ {1,2} is not a well-formed statement under ordinary typed arithmetic because 2 is an integer, not a set of integers. Conversely {2} ⊆ {1,2}, while {2} ∈ {1,2} is false. Some set-theoretic foundations encode numbers as sets; that encoding does not erase the intended types in a discrete-mathematics problem.

To disprove A ⊆ B, exhibit a witness x ∈ A with x ∉ B. To disprove A = B, one witness in the symmetric difference suffices. To prove A ⊊ B, first prove containment and then give a member of B outside A. Showing one common member or a diagram that “looks contained” is insufficient.

3. The algebra of finite set operations

3.1 Exact membership tests

Fix a universe U containing all sets under discussion whenever a complement is used. For x ∈ U:

Operation Membership statement Meaning
A ∪ B x ∈ A or x ∈ B Inclusive or; common members appear once.
A ∩ B x ∈ A and x ∈ B Members shared by both.
A ∖ B x ∈ A and x ∉ B Remove B's members from A.
Ac = U ∖ A x ∈ U and x ∉ A Relative complement in U.
A △ B exactly one of x ∈ A, x ∈ B Symmetric difference, (A ∖ B) ∪ (B ∖ A).

The expression A ∖ B is generally different from B ∖ A; it is not numerical subtraction. The operations ∪ , ∩ , and △ are commutative. Complement changes if U changes: with A = {1} and U = {1,2}, Ac = {2}; with U = {1,2,3}, it is {2,3}. Never cancel or complement sets before establishing their universe.

The four regions determined by A and B in U are A ∩ B, A ∖ B, B ∖ A, and U ∖ (A ∪ B). They are pairwise disjoint and their union is U. Every two-set identity can be checked region by region. For three sets there are eight membership patterns (the three yes/no choices), a useful finite model for finding a counterexample. A region diagram is an aid to discovery, while membership arguments and the Boolean-pattern table provide the proof.

3.2 Laws and a proof strategy

Under the fixed universe U, the following laws are elementwise versions of the propositional laws already studied:

Law Set identity
Identities A ∪ ∅ = A; A ∩ U = A.
Domination A ∪ U = U; A ∩ ∅ = ∅.
Idempotence A ∪ A = A; A ∩ A = A.
Complements A ∪ Ac = U; A ∩ Ac = ∅; (Ac)c = A.
Commutativity A ∪ B = B ∪ A; A ∩ B = B ∩ A.
Associativity (A ∪ B) ∪ C = A ∪ (B ∪ C); likewise for ∩ .
Distributivity A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C); A ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C).
Absorption A ∪ (A ∩ B) = A; A ∩ (A ∪ B) = A.
De Morgan (A ∪ B)c = Ac ∩ Bc; (A ∩ B)c = Ac ∪ Bc.

For example, x ∈ A ∩ (B ∪ C) iff [x ∈ A and (x ∈ B or x ∈ C)] iff [(x ∈ A and x ∈ B) or (x ∈ A and x ∈ C)] iff x ∈ (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C). This proof explicitly maps ∩ to “and” and ∪ to inclusive “or.” To negate membership, use De Morgan on the whole condition. For example, A ∖ (B ∪ C) = (A ∖ B) ∩ (A ∖ C), whereas (A ∖ B) ∪ (A ∖ C) = A ∖ (B ∩ C). A parenthesis error swaps the two results.

Symmetric difference is associative because membership is exclusive-or: x ∈ (A △ B) △ C iff an odd number of the three membership statements is true, iff x ∈ A △ (B △ C). Also A △ A = ∅, A △ ∅ = A, and A △ B = (A ∪ B) ∖ (A ∩ B). A △ B = ∅ iff A = B. A △ B = U iff B = U ∖ A. These follow region by region; they do not require A and B to be disjoint.

3.3 Containment, monotonicity, and disjointness

A ⊆ B iff A ∩ B = A iff A ∪ B = B. Prove the forward direction by membership; for the reverse, if A ∩ B = A, every x ∈ A belongs to A ∩ B and hence B. Equivalently, A ∖ B = ∅. These are useful decision rules when an expression contains a hidden containment assertion.

If A ⊆ B, then A ∪ C ⊆ B ∪ C and A ∩ C ⊆ B ∩ C. Complement reverses containment: Bc ⊆ Ac. Difference is monotone in its left argument but antitone in its right: A ⊆ B implies A ∖ C ⊆ B ∖ C, while C ⊆ D implies A ∖ D ⊆ A ∖ C. State the direction before manipulating a difficult inequality. A and B are disjoint iff A ∩ B = ∅; neither set needs to be empty. Pairwise disjoint sets have no element in any two distinct members of the family.

4. Families, products, and finite size

4.1 Indexed families, including an empty index set

An indexed family (Ai)i ∈ I assigns a set to each index i ∈ I. Its union contains x iff at least one i ∈ I satisfies x ∈ Ai; its intersection contains x iff every i ∈ I satisfies x ∈ Ai. These are quantified membership tests:

x ∈ ⋃i ∈ IAi ⇔ ∃i ∈ I: x ∈ Ai;  x ∈ ⋂i ∈ IAi ⇔ ∀i ∈ I: x ∈ Ai.

Repeated set values at different indices do not alter the union or intersection. With a common universe U, ⋃i ∈ ∅Ai = ∅ and ⋂i ∈ ∅Ai = U: the existential condition is false and the universal condition is vacuously true for every x ∈ U. Without a declared U, the empty intersection has no canonical set value in ordinary set theory. Do not replace it by ∅. Generalized De Morgan, under U, gives (⋃i ∈ IAi)c = ⋂i ∈ IAic and its dual, even for I = ∅ under these conventions.

If I is empty, “each Ai is nonempty” holds vacuously but gives no member of ⋂Ai; the latter depends on U. If I is nonempty and each Ai is nonempty, their intersection can still be empty: {1} ∩ {2} = ∅. Moving an existential choice outside a universal claim is generally invalid. For example, every Ai may have some member, but there need not be one member common to all Ai.

4.2 Cartesian products and ordered tuples

The Cartesian product A × B = {(a,b):a ∈ A and b ∈ B}. Equality of ordered pairs means (a,b) = (c,d) iff a = c and b = d. Hence A × B and B × A generally differ as sets, even when their finite sizes agree. A × ∅ = ∅ × A = ∅. A2 abbreviates A × A; An denotes length-n sequences with entries in A. The n = 0 case contains the one empty tuple, so A0 has one element even if A = ∅, under the standard sequence convention. For n>0, ∅n = ∅.

Products distribute over union and intersection in the factor being varied:

A × (B ∪ C) = (A × B) ∪ (A × C);  A × (B ∩ C) = (A × B) ∩ (A × C).

The same holds on the left. For example, (a,b) is in (A × B) ∩ (A × C) iff a ∈ A and b ∈ B and b ∈ C, iff (a,b) ∈ A × (B ∩ C). A more tempting formula, (A × B) ∩ (C × D) = (A ∩ C) × (B ∩ D), is also true by matching both coordinates. But A × B ⊆ C × D does not always imply A ⊆ C and B ⊆ D: if A or B is empty, the left product is empty whatever C and D are. If A and B are both nonempty, choose witnesses in the opposite factors to derive the two containments.

4.3 Power sets and cardinality

The power set P(A) = {S:S ⊆ A} is the set of all subsets of A. Always ∅ ∈ P(A) and A ∈ P(A). P(∅) = {∅}, which has one member; ∅ itself has zero. The distinction between ∈ and ⊆ becomes especially important here: S ∈ P(A) iff S ⊆ A, but S ⊆ P(A) means every member of S is itself a subset of A. The statements are different.

If finite A has n elements, each element can be included or excluded independently in a subset, giving |P(A)| = 2n. More specifically, the subsets of size k number C(n,k); summing over k yields ∑k = 0nC(n,k) = 2n. This identity is stated here as a connection; systematic combinations and counting proofs belong to the counting chapter. For finite A,B, |A × B| = |A||B|. Also |A ∪ B| = |A|+|B|−|A ∩ B|. The subtraction corrects double counting, even if one set is empty. These formulas are not asserted for arbitrary infinite cardinals using ordinary integer arithmetic.

For three finite sets, count each element by its membership multiplicity to obtain

|A ∪ B ∪ C| = |A|+|B|+|C|−|A ∩ B|−|A ∩ C|−|B ∩ C|+|A ∩ B ∩ C|.

An element in exactly one set has coefficient 1. An element in exactly two has coefficient 2−1 = 1. An element in all three has coefficient 3−3+1 = 1. This verifies the formula without assuming pairwise disjointness. The general inclusion–exclusion theorem and advanced applications are deferred to the counting chapter.

Finally, A ⊆ B iff P(A) ⊆ P(B): if A ⊆ B, every subset of A is a subset of B; conversely, A ∈ P(A), so P(A) ⊆ P(B) forces A ∈ P(B), meaning A ⊆ B. For finite A, B, P(A ∩ B) = P(A) ∩ P(B). In contrast, P(A ∪ B) generally strictly contains P(A) ∪ P(B), because a mixed subset may draw elements from both sides without being wholly inside either.

Teaching through formulas and conceptual decisions

Solve a cardinality question by recovering disjoint atoms

For two finite sets, the disjoint pieces are the intersection, the part only in the first set, the part only in the second, and the outside. If their sizes are respectively t,a-t,b-t,N-a-b+t, every one must be nonnegative. Thus a proposed intersection must satisfy max(0,a+b-N)≤t≤min(a,b). This feasibility check comes before substitution into a formula.

For three sets, start with the triple intersection, subtract it from the pair intersections, and only then obtain the single-only regions. A pair intersection includes the triple intersection unless explicitly stated otherwise. The union is

|A∪B∪C|=|A|+|B|+|C|-|A∩B|-|A∩C|-|B∩C|+|A∩B∩C|.

Exactly one membership has size the sum of singleton sizes minus twice the sum of pair intersections plus three times the triple intersection. Exactly two memberships has size the sum of pair intersections minus three times the triple intersection. These coefficients follow by charging an object that occurs in one, two or three sets; they are not independent formulas to memorize without a region model.

Count sets of sets by translating the constraint

If A⊆S⊆B and A⊆B, each element of B∖A is independently optional: there are 2|B|-|A| choices. A size restriction |S|=k instead gives (|B|-|A|k-|A|). If the premise A⊆B fails, the answer is zero; negative exponents cannot repair an inconsistent constraint.

For a fixed ordered pair (A,B) of subsets of an n -element universe, each element has four membership states. A local rule eliminates forbidden states: A⊆B leaves three, A∩B=∅ leaves three, and both together leave two. A rule requiring at least one element in a particular state needs subtraction of the configurations avoiding that state. Thus a proper inclusion has 3n-2n pairs, not 3n-1.

Algebraic identities are truth-table identities

Set a=[x∈A], b=[x∈B], c=[x∈C]. Union, intersection, complement and symmetric difference become OR, AND, NOT and XOR. Equality of sets means equality on all admissible membership patterns. An implication between containments restricts which patterns are admissible; cancellation of a common union or intersection is generally invalid. A single legal pattern falsifying an identity is sufficient.

Detailed derivation tutorials

The following complete proofs and implementations support the new examination problems. They develop the reasoning needed to derive formulas; the separately labeled examination bank below tests calculation, concepts and distractor decisions.

The first problems rehearse exact syntax; later ones combine laws, quantifiers, finite counting, and counterexamples. The wording and solutions below are original, while the proof patterns are linked to the source texts in the references. Read the full solution after first following the membership conditions yourself; no answer is required from the student during the first reading.

Tutorial 1 — Nested emptiness and precise notation

Let A = {∅,{∅}}. Determine |A|, whether ∅ ∈ A, ∅ ⊆ A, {∅} ∈ A, {∅} ⊆ A, and whether {{∅}} ⊆ A. List P(A).

Solution. The two members of A are the empty set and the singleton containing the empty set; they are distinct, so |A| = 2. Both ∅ ∈ A and {∅} ∈ A are true by the roster. ∅ ⊆ A is true for every A. For {∅} ⊆ A, its sole member is ∅, and ∅ ∈ A, so it is true. For {{∅}} ⊆ A, its sole member is {∅}, which is also in A, so it is true. The four subsets are ∅, {∅}, {{∅}}, and {∅,{∅}}. Notice that {∅} occurs both as a member of A and as a subset of A, but those truths require different checks. The braces in {{∅}} create a third object, not a duplicate spelling of {∅}.

Tutorial 2 — Set builder and the domain trap

Let S = {x ∈ ℤ : x2≤8}, T = {x ∈ ℝ : x2≤8}, and V = {x ∈ ℤ : x2<9}. Decide S = V and S = T.

Solution. Among integers, x2≤8 permits x ∈ {−2,−1,0,1,2}; x2<9 permits exactly the same integers, so S = V. In the real domain, T = [−√8,√8], which includes 1/2 and infinitely many other nonintegers. Since 1/2 ∈ T but 1/2 ∉ S, S≠T. This single witness also proves T⊄S. Although S ⊆ T, the logical predicates alone do not determine equality without their domains.

Tutorial 3 — Proving equality by two inclusions

Prove A = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∖ B) for arbitrary sets A and B. Explain why disjointness matters.

Solution. If x ∈ A, either x ∈ B or x ∉ B. In the first case x ∈ A ∩ B; in the second x ∈ A ∖ B. Thus A ⊆ (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∖ B). Conversely, membership in either term implies membership in A, so the union is contained in A. The two inclusions give equality. Also (A ∩ B) ∩ (A ∖ B) = ∅, since membership would require x ∈ B and x ∉ B at once. Thus A has been partitioned into the part inside B and the part outside B; for finite A, their cardinalities add to |A|. This problem follows the two-containment and partition patterns shown in Cornell CS2800, with an independently written proof.

Tutorial 4 — A difference identity with every parenthesis visible

Prove A ∖ (B ∪ C) = (A ∖ B) ∩ (A ∖ C). Then identify the expression equal to (A ∖ B) ∪ (A ∖ C).

Solution. For arbitrary x, x ∈ A ∖ (B ∪ C) iff x ∈ A and x ∉ B ∪ C. The second condition means x ∉ B and x ∉ C, so the whole condition is (x ∈ A and x ∉ B) and (x ∈ A and x ∉ C), exactly membership in (A ∖ B) ∩ (A ∖ C). For the union, membership means (x ∈ A and x ∉ B) or (x ∈ A and x ∉ C). Distribute the common x ∈ A to obtain x ∈ A and (x ∉ B or x ∉ C), which by De Morgan is x ∈ A and x ∉ B ∩ C. Thus (A ∖ B) ∪ (A ∖ C) = A ∖ (B ∩ C). Replacing ∩ by ∪ in the last expression is the characteristic error.

Tutorial 5 — Conditional simplification versus cancellation

Assume A ⊆ B. Simplify A ∩ B, A ∪ B, A ∖ B, B ∖ A, and A △ B. Does A ∪ C = B ∪ C imply A = B?

Solution. Containment gives A ∩ B = A and A ∪ B = B. Since no member of A lies outside B, A ∖ B = ∅. The set B ∖ A cannot generally be simplified to ∅: take A = {1}, B = {1,2}. Because A ∖ B = ∅, symmetric difference reduces to B ∖ A. Union cannot be cancelled: take A = {1}, B = {2}, and C = {1,2}. Then A ∪ C = B ∪ C = C even though A≠B. The algebra of sets resembles Boolean algebra, not a cancellative group under union.

Tutorial 6 — Distributive law by element semantics

Prove A ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C), then give an explicit counterexample to the false formula A ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∪ B) ∩ C.

Solution. x ∈ A ∪ (B ∩ C) iff x ∈ A or (x ∈ B and x ∈ C). Distributivity of propositions changes this to (x ∈ A or x ∈ B) and (x ∈ A or x ∈ C), the right-hand membership condition. For the proposed false formula, let A = {1}, B = C = ∅. Its left side is {1}; its right side is ({1} ∪ ∅) ∩ ∅ = ∅. The missing A on the second factor loses elements that belong only to A. This is the dual set-distribution pattern; compare MIT 6.042J's elementwise treatment of the other direction.

Tutorial 7 — When does an inclusion become equality?

Prove A ∩ B ⊆ A ∪ B. Characterize exactly when A ∩ B = A ∪ B.

Solution. Every x ∈ A ∩ B is in both sets and hence in at least one, proving the inclusion. If A = B, both sides equal A, so equality holds. Conversely, assume A ∩ B = A ∪ B. For any x ∈ A, x ∈ A ∪ B and thus x ∈ A ∩ B, giving x ∈ B; hence A ⊆ B. Symmetrically B ⊆ A. Therefore A = B. The equality condition is stronger than merely having a nonempty intersection. With A = B = ∅ it still holds.

Tutorial 8 — Symmetric difference as parity

Let U = {1,2,3,4,5}, A = {1,2,4}, B = {2,3,4}, C = {1,3,5}. Compute (A △ B) △ C and A △ (B △ C), and explain why they agree generally.

Solution. A △ B = {1,3}. Hence (A △ B) △ C = {1,3} △ {1,3,5} = {5}. Next B △ C = {1,2,4,5}; A △ (B △ C) = {1,2,4} △ {1,2,4,5} = {5}. For any x, assign a bit to its membership in each set. Symmetric difference is bitwise exclusive-or, so x survives either grouped expression exactly when its three bits contain an odd number of ones. The agreement therefore holds for every x, including elements outside all three sets. A single numeric example illustrates but does not prove the general identity.

Tutorial 9 — Symmetric difference determines equality

Show A △ B = ∅ iff A = B. Then decide whether A △ B = A ∪ B iff A ∩ B = ∅.

Solution. If A △ B = ∅, there is no element exclusively in A or exclusively in B, so every x belongs to A iff it belongs to B; extensionality gives A = B. If A = B, no element belongs to exactly one, so the symmetric difference is empty. Also A △ B = (A ∪ B) ∖ (A ∩ B). If A ∩ B = ∅, removing it changes nothing, so A △ B = A ∪ B. Conversely, if these sets are equal and x were in A ∩ B, then x would be in A ∪ B but not in A △ B, a contradiction. The converse relies on a hypothetical common member, not on cardinalities.

Tutorial 10 — Indexed operations and decreasing tail sets

Let U = ℕ = {0,1,2,…}; for each n≥0 define An = {k ∈ ℕ:k≥n}. Find ⋃n≥0An, ⋂n≥0An, and the corresponding union and intersection when the index set is empty.

Solution. A0 = ℕ, so the union is ℕ. For the intersection, fix any k ∈ ℕ and choose n = k+1; then k ∉ An. No k is in all An, so the intersection is ∅. With no indices, there is no witness for existential membership, hence the union is ∅. Every x ∈ U satisfies the universal membership condition over an empty index set, hence the empty intersection is U = ℕ. The nonempty-index intersection ∅ and the empty-index intersection U are different questions. CMU's indexed-family material motivates this boundary check.

Tutorial 11 — Quantifier order hidden inside a family claim

For I = {1,2}, take A1 = {1} and A2 = {2}. Evaluate “∀i ∈ I ∃x ∈ Ai” and “∃x ∀i ∈ I (x ∈ Ai).”

Solution. The first statement is true: choose x = 1 for i = 1 and x = 2 for i = 2. The witness may depend on i. The second is false because it requires a single x ∈ A1 ∩ A2, but the intersection is empty. In set language, nonempty members of a family do not imply a nonempty common intersection. The attempted exchange of ∀ and ∃ is invalid; this is a logic error disguised as a set fact.

Tutorial 12 — Product distribution and the empty-factor exception

Prove (A × B) ∩ (C × D) = (A ∩ C) × (B ∩ D). Then decide if A × B ⊆ C × D implies A ⊆ C and B ⊆ D.

Solution. An ordered pair (x,y) belongs to the left side iff x ∈ A, y ∈ B, x ∈ C, and y ∈ D. Regrouping by coordinate gives x ∈ A ∩ C and y ∈ B ∩ D, exactly membership on the right. The proposed implication is false without nonemptiness: take A = {1}, B = ∅, C = ∅, D = {2}. Both products are empty, so containment holds; A ⊆ C is false and B ⊆ D is true. If A and B are nonempty and A × B ⊆ C × D, choose b0 ∈ B. For any a ∈ A, (a,b0) lies in C × D, so a ∈ C; thus A ⊆ C. Similarly choose a0 ∈ A to prove B ⊆ D. The nonempty witnesses are indispensable. This product-factor reasoning corresponds to CMU's Cartesian-products slides; the proof here uses ordered-pair membership at every step.

Tutorial 13 — Power sets, three different containments

Take A = {1,2} and B = {2,3}. Find P(A ∩ B), P(A) ∩ P(B), and P(A ∪ B). Give one member of P(A ∪ B) absent from P(A) ∪ P(B).

Solution. A ∩ B = {2}, so P(A ∩ B) = {∅,{2}}. A subset belongs to both P(A) and P(B) exactly when it is contained in both A and B, hence exactly when it is contained in A ∩ B; therefore P(A) ∩ P(B) = {∅,{2}}. The union A ∪ B = {1,2,3} has eight subsets. The mixed subset {1,3} is in P(A ∪ B) but neither P(A) nor P(B), because 3 ∉ A and 1 ∉ B. Thus P(A) ∪ P(B) is strictly smaller than P(A ∪ B) here. It is wrong to distribute P over ∪ as if P were an intersection or union symbol.

Tutorial 14 — A nested power-set test

Let A = {∅,{∅}}. Decide whether ∅ ∈ P(A), {∅} ∈ P(A), {∅} ⊆ P(A), and P(∅) ∈ P(A).

Solution. Since ∅ ⊆ A, ∅ ∈ P(A). Since ∅ ∈ A, the singleton {∅} is a subset of A, so {∅} ∈ P(A). To test {∅} ⊆ P(A), check its sole member ∅; it is in P(A), so this is true. Finally P(∅) = {∅}; this is already known to be a subset of A, hence P(∅) ∈ P(A). The four statements happen to be true here, but for four separate typed reasons. Replacing any ∈ by ⊆ without checking the objects would be invalid.

Tutorial 15 — Counting with overlapping sets

For finite sets A,B,C, suppose |A| = 18, |B| = 15, |C| = 12, |A ∩ B| = 6, |A ∩ C| = 5, |B ∩ C| = 4, and |A ∩ B ∩ C| = 2. Find |A ∪ B ∪ C| and the number in exactly two sets.

Solution. Inclusion–exclusion gives 18+15+12−6−5−4+2 = 32. The pairwise intersections each include the two members of the triple intersection. Hence exactly two sets contain (6−2)+(5−2)+(4−2) = 4+3+2 = 9 members. As a cross-check, exactly three has 2 and exactly one has 32−9−2 = 21. The seven internal Venn-region counts are nonnegative: AB-only 4, AC-only 3, BC-only 2, A-only 18−4−3−2 = 9, B-only 15−4−2−2 = 7, C-only 12−3−2−2 = 5, triple 2; their sum is 32. This check detects inconsistent data or arithmetic before an answer is accepted.

Tutorial 16 — Power-set monotonicity in both directions

Prove P(A) ⊆ P(B) iff A ⊆ B. Does P(A) = P(B) imply A = B?

Solution. If A ⊆ B, every S ⊆ A is also a subset of B by transitivity, so every S ∈ P(A) lies in P(B). Conversely, suppose P(A) ⊆ P(B). Because A ⊆ A, A ∈ P(A), hence A ∈ P(B); the definition of P(B) says A ⊆ B. If the power sets are equal, both subset directions hold and therefore A = B. Using the particular element A ∈ P(A) makes the reverse implication immediate; checking only singleton subsets would also work but would require more steps.

Tutorial 17 — Relative complements and generalized De Morgan

Let U = {1,2,3,4}, I = {1,2}, A1 = {1,2}, A2 = {2,3}. Verify (⋃i ∈ IAi)c = ⋂i ∈ IAic. Explain why the same law holds for I = ∅ under U.

Solution. The union is {1,2,3}, so its complement in U is {4}. The complements are {3,4} and {1,4}; their intersection is {4}. Generally, x lies outside the union iff there is no i with x ∈ Ai, iff for every i, x ∉ Ai, iff x belongs to every Aic. For I = ∅, the left side is (∅)c = U; the right side is the empty intersection, also U by the fixed-universe convention. Without U the complement and that empty intersection are not defined by this chapter's notation.

Tutorial 18 — A common false inference about differences

Is A ∖ C = B ∖ C enough to conclude A = B? If not, give a minimal counterexample and identify an additional condition under which it does follow.

Solution. No. With A = {1}, B = ∅, and C = {1}, both differences are ∅ but A≠B; removing C hides the disagreement. If both A and B are disjoint from C, then A ∖ C = A and B ∖ C = B, so equality of the differences does imply A = B. More generally, if A ∩ C = B ∩ C as well as A ∖ C = B ∖ C, the decomposition in Problem 3 gives A = (A ∩ C) ∪ (A ∖ C) = (B ∩ C) ∪ (B ∖ C) = B. The two conditions recover both the part inside C and the part outside it.

Tutorial 19 — A power-set identity and a false dual

Prove P(A ∩ B) = P(A) ∩ P(B). Find necessary and sufficient conditions for P(A ∪ B) = P(A) ∪ P(B).

Solution. For any set S, S ∈ P(A ∩ B) iff S ⊆ A ∩ B iff (S ⊆ A and S ⊆ B) iff S ∈ P(A) ∩ P(B). For the union identity, if A ⊆ B, then A ∪ B = B and P(A) ⊆ P(B), so both sides equal P(B); the same holds if B ⊆ A. Conversely, suppose neither A ⊆ B nor B ⊆ A. Choose a ∈ A ∖ B and b ∈ B ∖ A. Then {a,b} ⊆ A ∪ B, so {a,b} ∈ P(A ∪ B). But b ∉ A, so {a,b} ∉ P(A); and a ∉ B, so {a,b} ∉ P(B). Therefore equality fails. The identity holds exactly when A ⊆ B or B ⊆ A. This is a full characterization, not merely one counterexample.

Tutorial 20 — Checking a proposed identity with one membership pattern

Someone claims A △ (B ∩ C) = (A △ B) ∩ (A △ C). Decide whether it is an identity. If false, give a one-element universe counterexample and explain the pattern.

Solution. Let U = {x}, A = {x}, B = C = ∅. On the left, B ∩ C = ∅, so A △ (B ∩ C) = {x}. On the right, A △ B = A △ C = {x}, and their intersection is {x}; this pattern happens to agree, so it is not a counterexample. Try the pattern x ∉ A, x ∈ B, x ∈ C: take A = ∅ and B = C = {x}. The left side is ∅ △ {x} = {x}; the right side is ({x}) ∩ ({x}) = {x}, again agreement. Try x ∈ A, x ∈ B, x ∉ C: left side A △ ∅ = {x}; right side (A △ B) ∩ (A △ C) = ∅ ∩ {x} = ∅. Thus with A = B = {x}, C = ∅, the identity is false. The solution demonstrates a disciplined counterexample search: enumerate membership bits and reject candidate patterns that do not actually separate the sides. A Venn diagram alone can conceal this mistake.

From membership semantics to exact counting

The preceding definitions and proof tutorials describe when an individual object belongs to a set. Counting problems use those same definitions to describe which complete configurations are possible. A formula such as 3n is the end of a construction, not a substitute for identifying what its three alternatives mean. This section develops the constructions used in the question bank.

1. Encode a pair by disjoint membership regions

For A,B⊆U, every object has exactly one state: 00,10,01 or 11. These represent outside both, A only, B only and both. An assignment of states to all labelled objects determines the sets. Conversely, the sets determine every state. This correspondence is a bijection, so it neither omits nor duplicates pairs.

If the restriction merely permits a fixed set of r local states and places no further requirement on their populations, the count on an n -object universe is rn. The multiplication rule applies because choosing a permitted state for one object does not change the alternatives for another. For example, containment forbids 10, whereas full union forbids 00. Both leave three states, although they describe different pairs. If the restriction requires a particular state to occur, choices cease to be unrestricted: the all-other-states words must be excluded.

Pair condition Permitted states Count
None 00,10,01,11 4n
A⊆B 00,01,11 3n
A∪B=U 10,01,11 3n
A∩B=∅ 00,10,01 3n
Disjoint cover 10,01 2n

For a prescribed intersection I, objects inside and outside I have different alternatives. Inside objects are forced into 11; outside objects have three alternatives. The count is 3n-|I|. If only |I|=j is specified, first choose its members and obtain (nj)3n-j. The binomial factor is present only in the second problem.

2. Require witnesses by inclusion-exclusion

Consider contained pairs with ∅≠A⊊B⊊U. The three regions A, B∖A and U∖B must all be nonempty. Without that requirement there are 3n assignments. Let an event mean that one of the three regions is empty. Each event leaves two choices per object, and an intersection of two events leaves one. On a nonempty universe, all three events cannot occur together. Hence

3n-3·2n+3,n≥1.

At n=0 the answer is directly zero; extending this displayed expression would give one because its omitted three-event intersection is no longer empty. This illustrates why a parameter domain belongs to the derivation.

A strict nested triple A⊊B⊊C has four possible regions, but only B∖A and C∖B must be nonempty. Excluding the two missing-witness events gives 4n-2·3n+2n, valid even at zero. Do not require A to be nonempty unless the stem does. Strict containment asserts the existence of a difference witness, not the existence of an element of the smaller set.

3. Fixed populations require multinomial counting

Suppose a universe of size n is assigned to labelled disjoint regions of sizes r1,…,rk, with nonnegative integer sizes summing to n. Choose the first region, then the second from the remaining objects, and continue. The binomial factors telescope to

(nr1)(n-r1r2)…(rkrk)=n!r1!…rk!.

The factorial denominator removes the order of objects within each region. It does not identify different region labels. For sizes 2,1,1,2 on six objects the count is 6!/(2!1!1!2!)=180. The two regions of size two remain distinct; exchanging them changes membership. Summing multinomial counts over all permitted populations produces the corresponding unrestricted state count. This links the region method to the binomial and multinomial theorems rather than leaving them as unrelated shortcuts.

4. Recover all atoms before using cardinalities

For three sets, the eight disjoint atoms are their membership states 000 through 111. If t=|A∩B∩C|, the A,B -only population is |A∩B|-t. The A -only population is

|A|-|A∩B|-|A∩C|+t.

The triple intersection is added back because the two pair subtractions removed it twice although it occurred once in |A|. The analogous formulas recover the other exclusive atoms. The outside atom is |U|-|A∪B∪C|. Each atom must be a nonnegative integer. These conditions, together with the population sum, are both necessary and sufficient for a finite realization: allocate that many distinct labelled objects to each atom and reconstruct the sets.

If exactly-two membership is asked, add the three pair-only atoms:

|A∩B|+|A∩C|+|B∩C|-3t.

If at-least-two is asked, add t to this quantity instead. If exactly-one is asked, sum the three singleton atoms, giving the sum of single-set sizes minus twice the sum of pair sizes plus 3t. A diagram should display the recovered atom populations; an attractive overlap picture without those data cannot verify the calculation.

5. Count the objects, rather than their possible witnesses

A four-element subset of {1,…,10} contains an odd pair sum exactly when it contains at least one odd and one even number. A subset with two of each parity has four possible odd-even witness pairs. Choosing a witness pair first therefore counts this subset repeatedly, while a subset with one odd and three even elements has three witnesses. A single division factor cannot repair that unequal multiplicity.

Instead, count the failing objects: they contain only odd numbers or only even numbers. Each failure class contains (54)=5 subsets and the classes are disjoint. The result is (104)-2(54)=200. Alternatively, classify by the number of odd elements:

(51)(53)+(52)(52)+(53)(51)=50+100+50=200.

This positive enumeration independently checks the complement count. A witness-first method becomes valid only if witness multiplicities are controlled or the witness itself is part of the requested object.

6. Separate ordered pairs from exchange classes

For a family invariant under exchanging A,B, each pair with unequal coordinates belongs to a two-element exchange class. A pair with equal coordinates is fixed and belongs to a one-element class. If N is the ordered count and F the fixed count, the unordered count is F+(N-F)/2=(N+F)/2.

Covering pairs have N=3n and F=1, because equality and coverage force A=B=U. Complementary pairs on a nonempty universe have N=2n and F=0. Pairs with prescribed symmetric difference D have N=2n; they have no fixed points when D is nonempty and all pairs fixed when D is empty. Thus “divide by two” has different answers even when the ordered counts agree. A family not preserved by exchange, such as prescribed unequal exclusive-region sizes, cannot use this argument at all.

7. Keep the types of objects visible

In A∈P(B), the left object is itself a set, and the statement means A⊆B. In P(A)⊆P(B), arbitrary subsets of A must also be subsets of B. These statements are equivalent to A⊆B, but the quantification is over different objects.

For a transitive set S, every member of every member lies in S. Equivalently, ⋃S⊆S; equivalently, every member of S is a subset of S, so S⊆P(S). This does not mean that all subsets of S belong to S. For S={∅,{∅}}, the subset {{∅}} is missing as a member. Writing one row per brace level prevents replacing membership by containment or confusing transitivity with full downward closure. The question bank uses both elementwise proofs and explicit small families to make this distinction checkable.

This bank combines authentic Iranian entrance-examination questions, newly authored medium/hard analogues, and two retained multistep challenges. The original four-option numbering is retained for authentic questions. Difficulty labels for original problems are qualitative author judgments, not calibrated response statistics.

Question 1. MSc CS 1405, Q37 — Set-expression elimination

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 9 · question 37. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

Simplify (Ac∩B)∪[((A∖B)∪Bc)∩(B∖A)]. Complements are relative to the same universe.

1.
A
2.
B∖A
3.
A∖B
4.
B
Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 2. Write A∖B=A∩Bc and B∖A=B∩Ac. Any member of the second intersection would have to belong to B∖A and to (A∖B)∪Bc. The first requirement forces membership in B and nonmembership in A. The union's two alternatives then both fail: such an object belongs neither to A∖B nor to Bc. The second intersection is therefore empty. The first term is exactly B∩Ac=B∖A, so union with the empty term leaves that set unchanged.

Membership region First term Second intersection Whole expression
Outside both 0 0 0
A only 0 0 0
B only 1 0 1
Both 0 0 0

Option 1 includes the A -only region and excludes the B -only region. Option 3 selects the opposite exclusive region. Option 4 additionally includes the common region. For instance, A={1} and B={1,2} produce the result {2}, whereas options 1, 3 and 4 give {1}, the empty set and {1,2}. A short disjointness argument removes the complicated term without an unnecessary full distributive expansion.

Question 2. MSc CS 1405, Q101 — Two tests for a transitive set

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 22 · question 101. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

A set A is transitive when x∈y∈A implies x∈A. Consider (a) ⋃A⊆A and (b) A⊆P(A). Which of these conditions is equivalent to transitivity of A?

1.

Only (a).

2.

Only (b).

3.

Both.

4.

Neither.

Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 3. Expand transitivity rather than reasoning from the appearance of the symbols. If x∈⋃A, some y∈A contains x. Thus x∈y∈A, and transitivity gives x∈A. This proves ⋃A⊆A.

Now take an arbitrary y∈A. Every member x of y belongs to A, again by transitivity. Therefore y⊆A, meaning y∈P(A). Since the chosen member y was arbitrary, A⊆P(A).

Conversely, if the union inclusion holds, any x∈y∈A belongs to ⋃A and hence to A. If the power-set inclusion holds, any y∈A is a subset of A, so every x∈y belongs to A. Each condition individually characterizes transitivity, and both must hold. Options 1 and 2 omit an equivalent characterization; option 4 rejects both.

For a boundary check, the empty set is transitive and satisfies both inclusions. A useful counterexample to automatic transitivity is A={{∅}}: its union contains ∅, but ∅∉A, and its sole member is not a subset of A. Membership, subset inclusion and power-set membership must be translated at their actual brace levels.

Question 3. PhD CS 1405, Q18 — Transitivity of two small families

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 8 · question 18. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

A family S is acceptable if ⋃S⊆S. Let S1={∅,{∅}} and S2={∅,{∅},{∅,{∅}}}. Which families are acceptable?

1.

S1 only.

2.

S2 only.

3.

Both.

4.

Neither.

Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 3. Name the nested objects e=∅, s={e} and t={e,s}. Then S1={e,s} and S2={e,s,t}. Taking a union gathers the members of these objects, not the objects themselves.

Object in a family Its members contributed to the union
e None
s e
t e and s

Consequently ⋃S1={e}, a subset of S1, and ⋃S2={e,s}=S1, a subset of S2. Both families qualify. Neither equality ⋃Si=Si is required; in fact both displayed inclusions are proper.

Option 1 ignores the valid second inclusion. Option 2 ignores the valid first inclusion. Option 4 confuses the union's elements with one additional level of braces. To verify directly from the definition, inspect each member of each family: every member of those member-sets is already present as a member of the original family. This is exactly transitivity. The calculation also explains why adding {t} without adding t to a family could break the property: union would expose a missing member.

Question 4. PhD CS 1404, Q25 — A subset containing an odd pair sum

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 7 · question 25. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

How many four-element subsets A of {1,2,…,10} contain two elements x,y such that x+y is odd?

1.

200

2.

205

3.

208

4.

209

Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 1. Split the ten integers into five odd and five even objects. Two distinct selected elements have an odd sum exactly when their parities differ. Thus a four-element subset qualifies precisely when it contains at least one element of each parity.

There are (104)=210 unrestricted subsets. The failures are four odds, numbering (54)=5, or four evens, also numbering 5. The failure classes are disjoint, so the answer is 210-5-5=200.

A second calculation partitions by the exact number of selected odd elements:

(51)(53)+(52)(52)+(53)(51)=50+100+50=200.

Option 2 subtracts only one homogeneous parity class. Options 3 and 4 subtract respectively two and one subsets instead of the ten failures. Choosing a particular odd-even witness pair and then two other elements overcounts: a subset with two odds and two evens has four different witness pairs, whereas one with one odd and three evens has three. There is no uniform witness multiplicity by which to divide that naive count. Counting the property by its complement or by a disjoint parity partition avoids this issue.

Question 5. Recover exactly-two and outside counts

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1405_Q21. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Three subsets of a 60-element universe have sizes 25, 22, and 20. Their pairwise intersections have sizes 10, 9, and 8; the triple intersection has size 4. What are the numbers in exactly two sets and in none?

Required reasoning. Derive the answer from the stated regions or a bijection. Explain every choice, subtraction and boundary case, and distinguish the incorrect alternatives.

1.

15 and 16.

2.

27 and 16.

3.

15 and 20.

4.

19 and 16.

Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 1. The given pairwise intersection counts include the triple intersection. Subtract its size once from each pair to obtain the exclusive pair regions: 10-4=6, 9-4=5 and 8-4=4. Exactly-two membership is their disjoint sum, 6+5+4=15.

Three-set region Population
A only 25-10-9+4=10
B only 22-10-8+4=8
C only 20-9-8+4=7
A,B only 6
A,C only 5
B,C only 4
All three 4
Outside all three 60-44=16

Inclusion-exclusion gives union size 25+22+20-10-9-8+4=44, so sixteen objects are outside. Every region population is nonnegative and the eight populations sum to sixty, checking feasibility as well as arithmetic.

Option 2 uses the raw sum 27 of pair intersections and counts each triple member three times as if it had exactly two memberships. Option 3 drops the final triple correction in the union formula, producing outside count 20. Option 4 subtracts only two copies of the triple population from the pair sum, yielding 19 and still retaining one count for each triple member. Exactly-two counting removes all three copies, while union counting restores one after the pair subtractions.

Question 6. Two nested strict inclusions

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q120; MS_CS_1405_Q124. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

If |U|=5, how many ordered pairs (A,B) satisfy ∅≠A⊊B⊊U?

Required reasoning. Derive the answer from the stated regions or a bijection. Explain every choice, subtraction and boundary case, and distinguish the incorrect alternatives.

1.

150

2.

120

3.

180

4.

90

Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 1. The three disjoint labelled regions are A, B∖A and U∖B. Each must be nonempty: these express, respectively, the nonempty smaller set and the two proper containments. Conversely, any assignment of the five labelled objects to three nonempty regions reconstructs a unique valid pair by taking B to be the union of the first two regions.

Start with 35=243 assignments. Excluding each of three empty-region events removes 3·25=96. Each intersection of two empty-region events puts all objects in the remaining region and contributes one; there are three such intersections. All three regions cannot be empty because the universe has five objects. Therefore 243-96+3=150.

An independent size partition gives

∑a=13(5a)(25-a-2)=5·14+10·6+10·2=150.

After choosing A, select a nonempty proper part of its complement for B∖A. Option 3, 180, arises if the outside region is allowed to be empty while the first two are nonempty; it wrongly admits B=U. Options 2 and 4, 120 and 90, do not match the displayed nonempty-region partition. The labels matter: exchanging the first and last region changes the pair's roles, so dividing by a region-permutation factorial would count a different object.

Question 7. Power-set difference is not a power set

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q101; MS_CS_1405_Q37. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

|A|=4, |B|=3, and |A∩B|=2. What is |P(A)∖P(B)|?

Required reasoning. Derive the answer from the stated regions or a bijection. Explain every choice, subtraction and boundary case, and distinguish the incorrect alternatives.

1.

4

2.

8

3.

12

4.

16

Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 3. A subset belongs to both P(A) and P(B) precisely when every one of its elements belongs to both underlying sets. Hence

P(A)∩P(B)=P(A∩B).

There are 24=16 subsets of A, of which 22=4 are also subsets of B. Their difference therefore has twelve members. This subtraction operates on collections of subsets, not on the underlying objects directly.

For an explicit model, let A={1,2,3,4} and B={1,2,5}. A subset of A fails to be a subset of B exactly when it contains 3 or 4. Choose a nonempty subset of {3,4} in three ways and any subset of {1,2} in four ways, giving 3·4=12.

Option 1 counts only P(A∖B) and wrongly excludes mixed subsets such as {1,3}; it also includes the empty subset, which is not in the requested difference. Option 2, eight, would fix one particular exclusive element as included and misses qualifying subsets using only the other exclusive element. Option 4 fails to subtract shared subsets. The correct factorization is (2|A∖B|-1)2|A∩B|, not 2|A∖B|.

Question 8. A symmetric-difference cancellation

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q37; MS_CS_1405_Q99. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

|A|=11, |B|=9, and |A△B|=12. Find |A∩B| and |(A△B)△B|.

Required reasoning. Derive the answer from the stated regions or a bijection. Explain every choice, subtraction and boundary case, and distinguish the incorrect alternatives.

1.

4 and 11.

2.

8 and 11.

3.

4 and 12.

4.

4 and 9.

Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 1. Symmetric difference contains the exclusive regions and excludes the common region. Thus

12=11+9-2|A∩B|,

giving |A∩B|=4. The factor two comes from counting a common object once in each of |A| and |B| although symmetric difference must count it zero times.

Membership in symmetric difference is XOR. For an arbitrary object, let its membership bits in A and B be a,b. The bit in (A△B)△B is (a⊕b)⊕b=a, because toggling twice restores a bit. Hence the entire set equals A and has size eleven.

Option 2 forgets the factor two and gives an intersection size of eight. Option 3 retains the intermediate symmetric difference instead of applying the second toggle. Option 4 incorrectly returns B. This cancellation does not require disjointness. It does, however, require the same set B in both positions; replacing one occurrence by a different set invalidates the cancellation. The two parts of the problem use different evidence: a cardinality equation for the first and an elementwise identity for the second.

Question 9. An equation between unions imposes one missing region

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q37; Phd_CS_1405_Q21. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Fix B⊆U with |U|=8 and |B|=3. How many A⊆U satisfy A∪B=U and A∩B≠∅?

Required reasoning. Derive the answer from the stated regions or a bijection. Explain every choice, subtraction and boundary case, and distinguish the incorrect alternatives.

1.

7

2.

31

3.

56

4.

63

Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 1. The union equation forces every element of U∖B into A: otherwise that element belongs to neither set and the union misses it. These five objects contribute no choice. Inside B, at least one of the three objects must be chosen for A to make the intersection nonempty. Therefore A is uniquely of the form

A=(U∖B)∪S,∅≠S⊆B.

There are 23-1=7 possible sets S and hence seven possible sets A. No multiplier is needed for the five forced objects.

Option 2 counts nonempty selections from the wrong five-object region. Option 3, 56, counts a different product of three- and five-object choices despite the fixed outside region. Option 4 uses six independent bits, although only three membership bits are free. If the intersection were required to have exactly two elements, the answer would be (32)=3. If the intersection could be empty, all eight selections inside B would be allowed. If disjointness were added, only S=∅ would work, contradicting the nonempty intersection requirement and giving zero solutions.

Question 10. Transitivity versus downward closure of all subsets

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q101; Phd_CS_1405_Q18. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

For S={∅,{∅},{∅,{∅}}}, which is correct?

Required reasoning. Derive the answer from the stated regions or a bijection. Explain every choice, subtraction and boundary case, and distinguish the incorrect alternatives.

1.

⋃S=S and S=P(S).

2.

⋃S⊊S and S⊊P(S).

3.

⋃S⊈S.

4.

S⊈P(S).

Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 2. Again write e=∅, s={e} and t={e,s}. The given set is S={e,s,t}. Union exposes e from s and exposes e,s from t, so ⋃S={e,s}. This is a proper subset of S, since t is absent from the union.

Every member of S is a subset of S: e has no members, s contains only e, and t contains e,s. Thus S⊆P(S). It is proper because S has three members but its power set has eight. For an explicit missing member, {t} belongs to P(S) but is not one of e,s,t.

Option 1 wrongly makes both inclusions equalities. Option 3 contradicts the direct union list. Option 4 contradicts the member-by-member subset check. Transitivity states that every member is a subset of the original set; it does not state that every subset of the original set is a member. The latter downward-closure condition is stronger and fails in the example at {t}. Distinguish the two directions before reading a power-set inclusion as a closure property.

Question 11. Count a prescribed Venn-region population

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q120; Phd_CS_1405_Q21. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

U has six distinct elements. Count ordered pairs (A,B) with |A∖B|=2, |B∖A|=1, and |A∩B|=1.

Required reasoning. Derive the answer from the stated regions or a bijection. Explain every choice, subtraction and boundary case, and distinguish the incorrect alternatives.

1.

360

2.

180

3.

720

4.

90

Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 2. The four disjoint labelled regions are A∖B, B∖A, A∩B and U∖(A∪B). Their sizes are 2,1,1 and 6-2-1-1=2. A pair is reconstructed uniquely from its assignment of labelled objects to these regions.

Choose the two A -only objects in (62)=15 ways, the one B -only object from the remaining four in four ways, and the common object from the remaining three in three ways. The remaining two are forced outside. Thus 15·4·3=180, equivalently

6!2!1!1!2!=180.

Option 1, 360, misses one of the two factorial corrections for unordered elements within a size-two region. Option 3, 720, counts all element orderings without either correction. Option 4, 90, divides the correct count by an unjustified exchange of labelled roles. Equal region sizes do not make the regions interchangeable: A -only and outside-both encode different membership bits. Swapping A and B would also change the required exclusive sizes from (2,1) to (1,2), so it is not a symmetry of the stated family.

Question 12. A Cartesian-product identity with a boundary case

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q37; MS_CS_1405_Q40. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Which identity holds for every set C, including C=∅?

Required reasoning. Derive the answer from the stated regions or a bijection. Explain every choice, subtraction and boundary case, and distinguish the incorrect alternatives.

1.
(A∖B)×C=(A×C)∖(B×C)
2.
(A×C)∖(B×C)=(A∖B)×(C∖C)
3.
A×C=B×C⇒A=B
4.
(A∪B)×C=(A×C)∩(B×C)
Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 1. An ordered pair (a,c) belongs to (A∖B)×C exactly when a∈A, a∉B and c∈C. Membership in (A×C)∖(B×C) requires a∈A,c∈C and not (a∈B∧c∈C). Since c∈C already holds, the final condition reduces to a∉B. The two sides have identical membership conditions for every ordered pair, proving equality even when C is empty.

To reject option 2, take A={0}, B=∅ and C={1}. Its left side contains (0,1), while its right side is empty because C∖C is empty. To reject option 3, let C=∅ and choose unequal A,B: both products are empty, so product equality does not permit cancellation. To reject option 4, use the same one-object example with B=∅; its left product is nonempty and the proposed intersection empty.

If C is nonempty, product cancellation is valid: select one c∈C and use pairs (a,c) to prove both inclusions between A and B. That proof explains exactly why the empty factor is the boundary, rather than treating it as a memorized exception.

Element categories under containment

Question 13. Element categories under containment — exact instance 1

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q37; MS_CS_1405_Q101. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Let U be a fixed labelled universe of size n. Count ordered pairs of subsets satisfying A⊆B; equality and empty sets are permitted. Set n=5. What is the exact count?

Required reasoning. Derive the answer from the stated regions or a bijection. Explain every choice, subtraction and boundary case, and distinguish the incorrect alternatives.

1.
125
2.
243
3.
1024
4.
32
Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 2. For each of the five labelled objects, record its membership in A,B as a pair of bits. Containment forbids 10, because an object cannot be in A and outside B. The remaining states are 00, 01 and 11. The assignment of states determines the pair uniquely, and every such assignment satisfies containment. Independent choices for the five distinct objects therefore give 35=243.

One can verify the count by choosing B first. If |B|=b, there are (5b) choices of B and 2b choices of its subset A. Thus

∑b=05(5b)2b=1+10+40+80+80+32=243.

The term b=0 is important: the pair (∅,∅) is valid. Option 1, 53, chooses a labelled object three times and does not assign a membership state to every object. Option 3, 45, permits the forbidden state 10. Option 4, 25, counts only equal pairs A=B, whose objects have states 00 or 11. There are 243-32=211 proper-containment pairs, but proper containment was not required.

Question 14. Element categories under containment — exact instance 2

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q37; MS_CS_1405_Q101. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Let U be a fixed labelled universe of size n. Count ordered pairs of subsets satisfying A⊆B; equality and empty sets are permitted. Set n=8. What is the exact count?

Required reasoning. Derive the answer from the stated regions or a bijection. Explain every choice, subtraction and boundary case, and distinguish the incorrect alternatives.

1.
6561
2.
65536
3.
256
4.
512
Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 1. With eight labelled objects, the permitted membership states for A⊆B remain 00,01,11. For example, the first object can be outside both sets, the second in B only, and the third in both; these choices impose no restriction on the fourth. A complete eight-state assignment is equivalent to one valid ordered pair. Consequently the count is 38=6561.

The independent binomial calculation is

∑b=08(8b)2b=(1+2)8=6561.

For a chosen B, containment leaves 2|B| possibilities for A, not the same number for every B. This explains why multiplying the number of all sets B by an arbitrary fixed number of subsets is invalid.

Option 2, 48=65536, counts unrestricted ordered pairs and includes violations of containment. Option 3, 28=256, counts equal pairs only. Option 4, 512, does not describe the three-state choices or their binomial expansion; it cannot be justified by treating the two sets as a single eight-bit selection with one extra binary choice. Equality is allowed, so subtracting 256 would incorrectly enforce proper containment.

Question 15. Element categories under containment — symbolic generalization

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q37; MS_CS_1405_Q101. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Let U be a fixed labelled universe of size n. Count ordered pairs of subsets satisfying A⊆B; equality and empty sets are permitted. Assume n≥1. Which formula gives the count for every such n?

Required reasoning. Derive the answer from the stated regions or a bijection. Explain every choice, subtraction and boundary case, and distinguish the incorrect alternatives.

1.
4n
2.
2n
3.
n3
4.
3n
Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 4. The map from a contained ordered pair to a word of length n over {00,01,11} is a bijection. Injectivity holds because the bits recover both sets. Surjectivity holds because absence of 10 guarantees that every member of A is a member of B. Therefore there are 3n pairs for every finite labelled universe, including n=0.

For a small check, let U={u}. The three pairs are (∅,∅), (∅,{u}) and ({u},{u}). For U=∅, there is the single empty pair, agreeing with 30=1. The formula also follows from the binomial theorem:

∑B⊆U2|B|=∑b=0n(nb)2b=3n.

Option 1 allows all four membership states. Option 2 restricts every object to 00 or 11 and therefore counts equality. Option 3, n3, counts ordered triples of chosen objects rather than assignments to every object. Containment is an elementwise implication; a numerical condition such as |A|≤|B| does not imply it. For example, A={1} and B={2} satisfy that size condition but violate containment.

Question 16. Element categories under containment — applicability and boundary

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q37; MS_CS_1405_Q101. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Let U be a fixed labelled universe of size n. Count ordered pairs of subsets satisfying A⊆B; equality and empty sets are permitted. Which statement correctly distinguishes proper from non-strict containment?

Required reasoning. Prove or refute each alternative using precise membership conditions and a counterexample when needed.

1.

Proper containment has exactly the same count as containment.

2.

Every contained pair must have an empty smaller set.

3.

Proper containment requires subtracting pairs with equal sets.

4.

Containment permits all four membership states.

Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 3. Proper containment removes exactly the pairs with A=B from the 3n contained pairs. An equal pair is determined by its common set, so there are 2n equal pairs. Hence

#{(A,B):A⊊B}=3n-2n.

Equivalently, proper containment requires at least one object with state 01, in addition to excluding 10 everywhere. Excluding assignments with no 01 leaves only the two states 00,11, which is exactly the subtraction above.

Option 1 is false: on a one-object universe non-strict containment permits three pairs but proper containment only (∅,U). Option 2 is false: take U={1,2}, A={1} and B=U; the smaller set is nonempty. Option 4 is false because state 10 directly contradicts containment. For n=0 the count is 1-1=0, as the only two subsets coincide. Distinguish a local restriction, which forbids a state at every object, from a strictness requirement, which demands at least one witness in a particular region.

Two sets whose union is prescribed

Question 17. Two sets whose union is prescribed — exact instance 1

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q37; MS_CS_1405_Q101. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Let U be a fixed labelled universe of size n. Count ordered pairs of subsets satisfying A∪B=U. No intersection or nonemptiness restriction is imposed. Set n=5. What is the exact count?

Required reasoning. Derive the answer from the stated regions or a bijection. Explain every choice, subtraction and boundary case, and distinguish the incorrect alternatives.

1.
243
2.
32
3.
1024
4.
211
Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 1. The equation A∪B=U forbids state 00. Each of the five labelled objects must belong to A only (10), to B only (01), or to both (11). These three choices are independent, giving 35=243 ordered covering pairs.

Another derivation chooses A. Every object outside A is forced into B, while each object inside A may or may not belong to B. For a chosen A of size a, there are 2a choices of B. Summing gives

∑a=05(5a)2a=243.

Option 2, 32, counts disjoint covering pairs by allowing only 10,01; disjointness is an additional restriction. Option 3, 1024, counts unrestricted pairs and includes 00. Option 4, 211, subtracts the 32 disjoint coverings and therefore counts only covering pairs with a nonempty intersection. A common object is permitted but not compulsory. Both pairs (∅,U) and (U,U) are valid, demonstrating that neither nonemptiness of both sets nor disjointness follows from the union equation.

Question 18. Two sets whose union is prescribed — exact instance 2

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q37; MS_CS_1405_Q101. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Let U be a fixed labelled universe of size n. Count ordered pairs of subsets satisfying A∪B=U. No intersection or nonemptiness restriction is imposed. Set n=8. What is the exact count?

Required reasoning. Derive the answer from the stated regions or a bijection. Explain every choice, subtraction and boundary case, and distinguish the incorrect alternatives.

1.
256
2.
65536
3.
6305
4.
6561
Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 4. The eight objects each have one of the states 10,01,11. Once those states are fixed, the two sets are recovered without further choices. Thus 38=6561.

The number with empty intersection is 28=256, because a disjoint cover allows only 10 and 01. The number with nonempty intersection is therefore

38-28=6561-256=6305.

This decomposition checks the requested count: every cover belongs to exactly one of those two classes, and 256+6305=6561. Option 1 selects only the disjoint class. Option 2, 48, admits objects in neither set and therefore fails the coverage requirement. Option 3 selects only the nonempty-intersection class. Nothing in the question chooses either class, so they must be added.

For example, assigning all eight objects to 11 produces A=B=U, and assigning all to 01 produces A=∅,B=U. Both extremes are valid. The common-region size may be any integer from zero through eight, with the count for exactly j common objects equal to (8j)28-j; summing over j again yields 38.

Question 19. Two sets whose union is prescribed — symbolic generalization

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q37; MS_CS_1405_Q101. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Let U be a fixed labelled universe of size n. Count ordered pairs of subsets satisfying A∪B=U. No intersection or nonemptiness restriction is imposed. Assume n≥1. Which formula gives the count for every such n?

Required reasoning. Derive the answer from the stated regions or a bijection. Explain every choice, subtraction and boundary case, and distinguish the incorrect alternatives.

1.
4n
2.
3n-2n
3.
3n
4.
2n
Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 3. A covering ordered pair is a partition of the labelled objects into three labelled regions: A∖B, B∖A and A∩B. The regions may be empty. Conversely, each such region assignment reconstructs exactly one covering pair. Consequently the count is 3n.

The binomial decomposition by intersection size makes the reasoning explicit:

∑j=0n(nj)2n-j=(1+2)n=3n.

Choose the j common objects, then place each remaining object in exactly one of the two exclusive regions. Option 1 counts all four membership states, including uncovered objects. Option 2 excludes the 2n disjoint covers, although the problem permits them. Option 4 counts only those disjoint covers. At n=1 there are three possibilities, of which two are disjoint and one has a common object. At n=0 the unique pair is (∅,∅); the general formula still gives one. The labels A and B make ordered pairs the requested objects, so exchanging the sets is generally a different answer.

Question 20. Two sets whose union is prescribed — applicability and boundary

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q37; MS_CS_1405_Q101. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Let U be a fixed labelled universe of size n. Count ordered pairs of subsets satisfying A∪B=U. No intersection or nonemptiness restriction is imposed. Which statement correctly describes coverage, disjointness and exchange of the two set labels?

Required reasoning. Prove or refute each alternative using precise membership conditions and a counterexample when needed.

1.

An element may lie in neither set under full coverage.

2.

Adding disjointness reduces each element to two possible memberships.

3.

Union coverage already guarantees disjointness.

4.

The unordered count is always exactly half the ordered count.

Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 2. Adding A∩B=∅ removes state 11 from the covering states 10,01,11. The remaining two states assign each labelled object to exactly one of the sets. Hence there are 2n ordered pairs.

Option 1 incorrectly permits 00, which would leave an object outside the union. Option 3 confuses covering with disjoint covering: A=B=U covers any nonempty universe but is not disjoint. Option 4 cannot obtain unordered coverings by always dividing 3n by two, because the exchange map has a fixed point. Its only fixed covering pair is (U,U). All other covering pairs come in distinct exchanged pairs, so the unordered count is

1+3n-12=3n+12.

For a one-object universe the three ordered coverings produce two unordered coverings, not one and a half. For disjoint coverings of a nonempty universe, there is no fixed point and division by two is valid, giving 2n-1. On the empty universe there is one fixed empty pair, so that special case must again be treated directly. Determine the family and its exchange-fixed objects before applying a symmetry divisor.

Nested families of sets

Question 21. Nested families of sets — exact instance 1

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Let U be a fixed labelled universe of size n. Count ordered triples of subsets satisfying A⊆B⊆C. Containment need not be proper. Set n=5. What is the exact count?

Required reasoning. Derive the answer from the stated regions or a bijection. Explain every choice, subtraction and boundary case, and distinguish the incorrect alternatives.

1.
243
2.
32
3.
1024
4.
32768
Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 3. Containment A⊆B⊆C permits only the following membership triples:

State in A,B,C Region
000 Outside C
001 C∖B
011 B∖A
111 A

For instance, 101 is forbidden because membership in A would require membership in B. Every assignment of the five labelled objects to these four regions reconstructs a unique nested triple. Thus 45=1024.

Option 1, 35, omits one permitted region. Option 2, 25, counts triples with all three sets equal, permitting only 000 and 111. Option 4, 85, permits all eight triples of bits and ignores both containment implications. Equalities and empty sets are allowed; the valid triple (∅,∅,∅) and the valid triple (U,U,U) must not be excluded. If both containments were proper, the regions 001 and 011 would have to be nonempty and the count would instead be 45-2·35+25=570.

Let U be a fixed labelled universe of size n. Count ordered triples of subsets satisfying A⊆B⊆C. Containment need not be proper. Set n=8. What is the exact count?

Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 2. Each of the eight labelled objects has four possible entry positions in the chain: it enters at A, at B only onward, at C only, or never. Their membership triples are respectively 111,011,001,000. The entry choices are independent, so the answer is 48=65536.

Choosing the largest set first gives a separate verification. For a specified C of size c, each of its objects has one of three states in the contained pair A⊆B⊆C, while objects outside C are forced outside both smaller sets. Hence

∑c=08(8c)3c=(1+3)8=65536.

Option 1, 256, counts the equal triples only. Option 3, 88=16777216, counts unrestricted triples, including 100 and 010, which violate the chain. Question 23. Nested families of sets — symbolic generalization

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q37; MS_CS_1405_Q101. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Let U be a fixed labelled universe of size n. Count ordered triples of subsets satisfying A⊆B⊆C. Containment need not be proper. Assume n≥1. Which formula gives the count for every such n?

Required reasoning. Derive the answer from the stated regions or a bijection. Explain every choice, subtraction and boundary case, and distinguish the incorrect alternatives.

1.
4n
2.
8n
3.
3n
4.
2n
Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 1. Under the chain condition, the membership bits of any object are nondecreasing when read from A to C. The only length-three nondecreasing binary words are 000,001,011,111. Thus the complete triple is equivalent to a length- n word over four states and its count is 4n.

On a one-object universe these words give exactly four nested triples; on an empty universe there is exactly one. Both checks agree with the formula. An alternative expression is

∑c=0n(nc)∑b=0c(cb)2b=∑c=0n(nc)3c=4n.

Here the inner sum first selects B within a fixed C, then selects A within B. Option 2 permits all eight local states. Option 3 incorrectly leaves only three states, as though one of the four regions were forbidden. Option 4 retains only the two equal-membership states. For a chain of k labelled sets the same argument gives (k+1)n, because a membership word can switch from zero to one at just one entry position, or remain zero throughout.

Question 24. Nested families of sets — applicability and boundary

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q37; MS_CS_1405_Q101. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Let U be a fixed labelled universe of size n. Count ordered triples of subsets satisfying A⊆B⊆C. Containment need not be proper. Which statement gives the correct way to count membership states in a chain of labelled sets?

Required reasoning. Prove or refute each alternative using precise membership conditions and a counterexample when needed.

1.

Nesting allows all eight three-bit patterns.

2.

All sets in a chain must be equal.

3.

Each extra set in the chain doubles the number of element states.

4.

For a chain of labeled sets, count entry positions rather than arbitrary bit patterns.

Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 4. In a chain of k sets, an object's membership can begin at any of the k sets, or at none of them. Once the object enters, it belongs to all later sets. There are therefore k+1 states, not 2k unrestricted bit patterns.

Option 1 ignores the forbidden patterns of a three-set chain; for example 100 violates A⊆B. Option 2 is refuted by A=∅, B={1}, C={1,2}, a valid chain whose sets differ. Option 3 is refuted by comparing a one-set chain, with two entry states, to a two-set chain, with three states rather than four.

Strictness is a global witness condition. For A⊊B⊊C, one must use state 011 at least once and state 001 at least once. Inclusion-exclusion gives

4n-2·3n+2n.

The two subtracted terms correspond to a missing first or second difference region; their intersection leaves only 000 and 111 and is restored once. It is wrong to forbid 000 or 111, or to require each object to witness strictness. For n=1 the count is zero because two distinct nonempty difference regions cannot be formed from one object.

Prescribed symmetric difference

Question 25. Prescribed symmetric difference — exact instance 1

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q37; MS_CS_1405_Q101. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Let U be a fixed labelled universe of size n, and let D⊆U be a prescribed set. Count ordered pairs satisfying A△B=D. Set n=5. What is the exact count?

Required reasoning. Derive the answer from the stated regions or a bijection. Explain every choice, subtraction and boundary case, and distinguish the incorrect alternatives.

1.
32

Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 1. The equation A△B=D determines B uniquely once A is selected:

B=A△D.

Indeed, XORing both sides with A cancels A△A=∅. Conversely, substituting this expression for B gives A△(A△D)=D. Thus every one of the 25=32 choices of A produces exactly one valid ordered pair.

For an object outside D, the two membership bits must agree, giving choices 00 or 11. For an object in D, they must differ, giving choices 01 or 10. There are two choices in either case, so the size of D does not change the count. Option 2 uses three states per object as though there were a containment or union restriction. Option 3 uses all four states and ignores the fixed XOR result. Option 4, 16, would count unordered pairs when D is nonempty; the question asks for ordered pairs. If D=∅, every solution has A=B and even the unordered count remains 32.

Correct option: 4. There are 28=256 choices for A. For each, the only possible second set is A△D, so the total is 256, regardless of how many of the eight objects are in the fixed set D.

Question 28. Prescribed symmetric difference — applicability and boundary

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CS_1405_Q37; MS_CS_1405_Q101. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Let U be a fixed labelled universe of size n, and let D⊆U be a prescribed set. Count ordered pairs satisfying A△B=D. Which statement correctly describes symmetric difference with a prescribed set?

Required reasoning. Prove or refute each alternative using precise membership conditions and a counterexample when needed.

1.

The number depends on the cardinality of the fixed set.

2.

The map taking a set to its symmetric difference with a fixed set is a bijection.

3.

Symmetric difference with a fixed set is always idempotent.

4.

A prescribed difference leaves both sets independent.

Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 2. Define TD(A)=A△D. Applying it twice gives

TD(TD(A))=(A△D)△D=A.

Thus TD is an involution. It is injective because applying it again to an equality of outputs recovers equality of inputs. It is surjective because TD(TD(B))=B supplies an input for every target B.

Option 1 is false: both empty and full D give two choices per object, so the ordered-pair count stays 2n. Option 3 confuses an involution with an idempotent operation. Take U=D={1} and A=∅. Then TD(A)={1}, whereas TD(TD(A))=∅; the two outputs differ. The identity TD2=TD holds for every input only when D=∅. Option 4 is false because the second set is uniquely determined by the first.

A fixed point would satisfy A△D=A and therefore D=∅. Hence nonempty D has no fixed points and the unordered solution count is 2n-1, while empty D fixes every subset and gives 2n unordered equal pairs. These are different counting problems from the ordered one.

1.
30

31

Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 1. A five-object universe has 25=32 subsets. Remove the empty set, which violates nonemptiness, and the full universe, which violates properness. They are distinct, so there are 32-2=30 eligible subsets.

Grouping by size verifies the subtraction:

(51)+(52)+(53)+(54)=5+10+10+5=30.

Option 2, 31, removes only one extreme and therefore describes either all nonempty subsets or all proper subsets, rather than both conditions. Option 3, 16, is the number of subsets with a specified object included, or half the complete power set; neither restriction is the question's condition. Option 4, five, counts singleton subsets only and omits valid larger subsets such as {1,2}.

The conditions are logically independent on a nonempty universe: the empty set is proper but not nonempty, and the full universe is nonempty but not proper. Complementation exchanges the nonempty proper subsets in distinct pairs. Since U is nonempty, no subset equals its own complement, so there are fifteen complementary pairs. That is a count of pairs of subsets, not the thirty individual subsets requested here.

2.

3.

Read the complete derivation and option analysis

Correct option: 2. On the empty universe the only subset is ∅=U. It is neither nonempty nor proper, so the desired family is empty. The usual subtraction 2n-2 is not valid at n=0, because its two excluded subsets coincide.

Option 3 is false because the empty set is a subset of every set: there is no element of it that can violate containment.
